summary: DNS Cookies are a lightweight transaction security mechanism giving limited protection to DNS servers and clients against denial-of-service, amplification, forgery and cache poisoning by off-path attackers. They tolerate NAT and anycast and can be deployed incrementally. This standards-track RFC defines them.

eli5.summary: A secret handshake token so a server can tell that a request really came from the sender it claims.

questions: what is the dns cookie option code
how do dns cookies stop amplification attacks
subtitle: A small token in each DNS message that lets servers and clients spot forged traffic from attackers who cannot see the conversation.

tldr.problem: DNS requests and replies are easy to forge. Off-path attackers can use forged source addresses to aim amplified traffic at a victim, load a server with work, or poison a resolver's cache.
tldr.mechanism: Each side adds a COOKIE option to its DNS messages. The client sends an 8-byte Client Cookie, the server answers with a Server Cookie, and later messages carry both, so each side can weakly check who it is talking to.
tldr.outcome: The protection is deliberately light. It stops off-path attackers but not attackers who can see the traffic. It was later updated by RFC 9018.

today: RFC 7873 is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 9018, so read the two together. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: The Threats DNS Cookies Address
sections.content:
RFC 7873 describes DNS Cookies, a lightweight transaction security mechanism carried as an option in the DNS OPT record. It targets off-path attackers, meaning attackers who cannot observe the request and response messages between a particular client and server.

Three problems are in scope. In an amplification attack, a short request with a forged source address makes a server send a much longer response to the victim. In a server denial of service, forged requests make a server do work, such as recursive queries or DNSSEC cryptography, before it can tell who is asking. In cache poisoning, forged replies are sent to a resolver, as in the Dan Kaminsky attack, hoping one is accepted.

Cookies do not stop on-path floods that use correct source addresses. They do help confirm the real source address, which makes it easier to contact the network involved.
sections.eli5: Bad guys can write a fake return address on a letter, so the reply goes to someone else. Cookies help the receiver notice fake return addresses.

sections.title: Why Existing DNS Security Was Not Enough
sections.content:
DNSSEC protects the data and can strongly resist forged data and cache poisoning. The RFC notes that it can make some denial-of-service attacks worse, because of the computation it needs and the larger responses it tends to produce.

TSIG could give stronger protection, but it needs pre-agreement and key distribution between client and server, server-side key state and time synchronization. TKEY can help with keys, but some modes are computationally heavy. SIG(0) authenticates complete transactions but not requests, and needs costly public key operations.

None of these gives what cookies give: lightweight message authentication of requests and responses with no pre-configuration and no per-client server-side state.
sections.eli5: Other lock systems exist, but they are heavy and need keys handed out ahead of time. Cookies are a light lock that needs no setup.

sections.title: The COOKIE Option
sections.content:
The COOKIE option lives in the OPT record of DNS requests and responses and uses option code 10. Its length tells which of two forms it is.

When the client does not yet know the server's cookie, the option is 8 bytes: just a Client Cookie. When a Server Cookie is known, and in all responses to such a request, the option is 16 to 40 bytes: the 8-byte Client Cookie followed by a Server Cookie of 8 to 32 bytes.

The Client Cookie SHOULD be a pseudorandom function of the Client IP Address, the Server IP Address and a Client Secret with at least 64 bits of entropy. The Server Cookie SHOULD include a 64-bit or larger pseudorandom function of the client's IP address, a Server Secret and the Client Cookie. The function is private to each side, since only its owner must recognize its own cookies. A client MUST send Client Cookies that usually differ for servers at different addresses.
sections.eli5: The client writes a secret code on its note. The server adds its own secret code. Both codes together prove who is who.

sections.title: How Clients and Servers Use Cookies
sections.content:
A client that supports cookies puts a COOKIE option in every request. If it has a cached Server Cookie for that server address, it sends the long form; otherwise it sends the short form.

A server where cookies are enabled treats the request one of five ways. With no COOKIE option it responds as if it did not implement cookies. A malformed option gets FORMERR; valid lengths are 8 and 16 to 40 inclusive. With only a Client Cookie, or an invalid Server Cookie, the server by policy (including rate limiting) may silently discard the request, send a BADCOOKIE error, or answer normally, and in the latter two cases it includes a fresh Server Cookie. Servers MUST at least occasionally respond so clients can learn the right Server Cookie. With a valid Server Cookie, the server can drop its defences against spoofed UDP requests and processes the request.

A client MUST discard a response with an illegal COOKIE length or a wrong Client Cookie, and a response that should carry the option but does not. It caches the Server Cookie from a good response, even an error one. On BADCOOKIE it SHOULD retry with the new Server Cookie, and if that also fails, SHOULD retry over TCP.

Section 5.4 adds a way to fetch a Server Cookie directly: a QUERY with an empty Question Section (QDCOUNT of zero) and a COOKIE option.
sections.eli5: The first time, the server hands the client a stamp. After that, the client shows the stamp each visit, and the server knows it is the same visitor.

sections.title: NAT, Anycast and Secret Rollover
sections.content:
Many clients behind a NAT box can share one outside address. That is why the Server Cookie is computed from the Client Cookie as well as the client address: otherwise a bot behind the NAT could learn a Server Cookie and use it with forged requests for other hosts. It also means the Client Cookie must stay stable for a server, so it must not depend on something like the request ID.

For anycast servers, either all clones MUST effectively agree, or requests from one client must reach one machine long enough. The RFC RECOMMENDS that anycast servers share the same Server Secret.

Secrets must be replaced regularly. The default lifetime is one day and the maximum permitted is one month. They MUST NOT be used in new messages for more than 36 days and SHOULD NOT be for more than 26 hours. Pseudorandom jitter of plus zero to minus at least 40% is RECOMMENDED to avoid synchronized rollovers. A server SHOULD accept its previous secret for a period of 1 to 300 seconds, default 150 seconds.

Cookies can be deployed one side at a time. A cookie-aware party interoperates with one that is not, but gets no benefit from it.
sections.eli5: Many kids sharing one house phone could confuse the receiver, so the stamp also depends on each kid's own code. Stamps are also swapped for new ones often, so a stolen stamp stops working.

sections.title: Limits and Security Considerations
sections.content:
DNS Cookies are a weak form of authentication. They give no protection against on-path adversaries, which means anyone who can observe the plaintext DNS traffic. Bypassing them takes guessing a 64-bit pseudorandom cookie, compared with the 32-bit TCP sequence number an attacker must guess to bypass TCP.

Servers still need other measures, such as rate limiting, against attackers who omit the option or send random Server Cookies. If bad cookies start to rise, an operator should consider rolling secrets over more often.

The cookie algorithm SHOULD be at least as strong as 64-bit FNV. The RFC says a strong cryptographic hash may not be warranted, but allows one, for example HMAC-SHA-256 truncated to 64 bits. Cookies cannot be used to generally track users, because they are only returned to the address they were received from.
sections.eli5: The stamp stops strangers far away from faking notes. It does not stop someone standing right next to you who can see the stamp.

sections.title: IANA Assignments
sections.content: IANA assigned EDNS0 option code 10, named COOKIE, with status Standard. It also assigned RCODE 23, BADCOOKIE (Bad/missing Server Cookie), as an early allocation.
sections.eli5: The official list of numbers now has an entry for cookies and one for the error that says the cookie was wrong.

messages.label: Request + Client Cookie
messages.note: Short form; no Server Cookie is known yet.

messages.label: Response + Client and Server Cookie
messages.note: A normal answer or BADCOOKIE, depending on server policy.

messages.label: Request + both cookies
messages.note: Long form, with the cached Server Cookie.

messages.label: Response + COOKIE option
messages.note: Processed normally; the server copies or regenerates the option.
